detail.abstract: Financial representatives increasingly communicate with retail investors through broadcasting technologies, such as mutual fund live streaming, which deliver one message to many retail investors instead of tailoring advice to each investor privately. This paper studies how broadcasting changes the strategic transmission of muddled information, that is, a message that mixes a financial product's intrinsic quality with the representative's skill at embellishing it. We analyze a signaling game model, in which a financial representative privately observes a financial product's intrinsic quality and her own promotional skill, then sends a noisy quality signal. Retail investors choose how much to rely on the signal when making investment decisions. We show that broadcasting induces more signal manipulation and, unexpectedly, stronger investor reliance on the manipulated signal. The mechanism is that each retail investor in a mass audience has limited power to discipline the representative's signal manipulation behavior, so each continues to rely on it. As a result, under the same regulatory stringency, broadcasting makes both the representative and investors worse off than one-to-one communication. However, broadcasting does not always call for stricter regulation: it calls for less stringent external regulation than the one-to-one channel when market self-regulation complements external regulation, and more stringent regulation when the two are substitutes. Our work provides implications for regulating the emerging adoption of muddled financial information broadcasting.

detail.abstract: In populations of language-model agents, an opinion reaches a listener only after a generator model has turned it into text and an appraiser model has turned the text back into a number, and this round trip distorts it. Motivated by such generator--appraiser architectures, we study a Friedkin--Johnsen model on a directed network in which committed agents form a boundary and every transmitted opinion passes through a monotone, saturating, speaker- and listener-dependent channel. The analysis separates four regimes. For small committed signals and subcritical interiors, the response is a Friedkin--Johnsen Green operator with gain-weighted edges. At finite amplitude, amplifying channels can violate the maximum principle of the linear model even without any instability. When the gain-weighted interior operator of a particular experiment is irreducible and has spectral radius above one, the response to a vanishing committed source no longer vanishes; for saturating channels the interior then has exactly one positive and one negative committed state, both stable within their sign cones, and an ordered population resists weak opposing sources. In the strong-gain limit, source-indexed broadcasting and reception scores degenerate and retain only reachability and susceptibility. We characterize committed-minority tipping by an explicit spinodal condition whose mean-field threshold grows as $(g/g^*-1)^{3/2}$. Reversing an ordered population is a finite-amplitude task, and infinitesimal response is a poor guide to it: on the empirical and synthetic networks studied, simple out-strength targeting reverses an ordered population as effectively as response-based rules, whereas rankings derived from the linearization at the ordered state, including its exact local response to clamping, perform markedly worse and in some networks close to random placement. The proposed framework is a theoretical model motivated by language-mediated communication; we do not fit it to LLM data.

detail.abstract: How do different modes of working with generative AI (GenAI) affect productivity and the experience of human workers and consumers? In this work, we examine three collaboration modes: AI-first (AI drafts, humans revise), human-first (humans draft, AI revises), and no-AI, in the context of professional writing tasks with 1,004 participants. We find that working with GenAI increased task completion time by 26% (AI-first) and 56% (human-first), due to time spent reviewing and fixing AI-generated content. Workers reported lower perceived autonomy and competence under the AI-first mode than the human-first mode. AI-assisted writing products were 60%-85% longer, more complex, and required about two higher grade levels to comprehend. Finally, a random exposure to a collaboration mode increased workers' likelihood of choosing the same mode for similar tasks in the future. Together, our findings highlight the importance of AI collaboration mode choice and the hidden costs of GenAI use on human experience.

detail.abstract: Regulators increasingly require insurers to demonstrate that their rating algorithms do not unfairly discriminate with respect to protected attributes, but they have not specified how such assessments should be conducted. This paper develops an operative criterion and a diagnostic framework for this task. We first discuss why, in insurance ratemaking, unfairness originates primarily in the information the fitted model uses rather than in biased outcome labels or historical human decisions. We then propose a residual-distribution fairness criterion: conditional on the admissible rating variables, the distribution of pricing errors should not depend on protected group membership. Comparing distributions rather than averages matters because insurance transfers the residual risk from the policyholder to the insurer, so that groups with equal average pricing errors can face economically different residual lotteries. We implement the criterion using surrogate residuals, which share a common standard normal reference distribution under correct model specification. The resulting diagnostic distinguishes misfit shared across groups from group-specific disparities and from differences in risk composition, localizes these disparities, and indicates the direction of mispricing. Using automobile insurance data, we demonstrate how the framework can be used to detect and localize disparities and to generate testable hypotheses about their sources.

detail.abstract:
Few stories in games are told as often as the comeback: a title launches to outrage, its developer keeps working, and years later the players return. The story usually treats three things as one: players forgiving the broken promises of launch, players judging the game favourably, and players coming back to play. We pulled these apart using the full public record of three high-profile launches: No Man’s Sky (2016), Cyberpunk 2077 (2020) and Starfield (2023). The data comprise 1,607,083 Steam reviews, ten years of Steam player counts, 111 dated developer events and US price histories. In 781,727 English reviews we tracked sentiment, complaints about technical quality and design, language of unmet expectations and deception, and trust directed at developers. We benchmarked every landmark release against Bayesian forecasts of the game’s own pre-release trajectory and tested the results with placebo dates, hold-out forecasts and prespecified sensitivity analyses. Checked against 390 reviews labelled with the help of a large language model and read independently by two of the authors, the keyword measures proved conservative: they seldom flagged reviews without the relevant content (specificity 0.96–0.99) but missed about half of those with it (sensitivity 0.41–0.58), and correcting for this error did not change the main patterns.
The comebacks began with anger and ended with repair. At No Man’s Sky’s launch, 8.6 of every 100 reviews accused the developer of lying, scamming or misleading players, and 20.9 spoke of unmet expectations; by year four these fell to 0.8 and 4.5, and its recommendation share rose from 54.2% to 91.9%. Cyberpunk 2077’s mainly technical complaints fell from 11.6 to 3.2 per 100 reviews as its share climbed to 94.8%. Starfield followed a different path. Its technical complaints also fell, but complaints about its design stayed at 18.1–22.2 per 100 reviews through three years and 9 substantial updates, more substantial updates per year than either comeback game received over the same period. Its design complaints grew with the time players invested, reaching 22.2 per 100 reviews among players with more than 100 hours, and its recommendation share settled near 60%. Engagement told a different story from evaluation. Every landmark release brought players back, with player numbers far above benchmark in the release month (No Man’s Sky +1366%, Cyberpunk 2077 +191%, Starfield +244%). The surge faded with a half-life of about one month, and only No Man’s Sky, which kept shipping large free updates, remained clearly above its earlier path a year later. Recommendation shares, by contrast, rose gradually and showed no detectable jump at any landmark release. General-purpose sentiment scores missed much of the recovery because satisfied reviewers increasingly wrote very short reviews. The recovery reflected changed minds, not only a changed reviewer pool: within group change explained 76% and 85% of the rise in No Man’s Sky’s and Cyberpunk 2077’s recommendation shares, and No Man’s Sky launch reviews that were revised years later now recommend the game 92.0% of the time, against 39.6% for launch reviews never revised. In these cases, a second chance was earned by repairing the specific failure that players complained about, not by the volume of updates or by a single spectacular release. Player attention responds within weeks, whereas player judgement changes only when the underlying problem is gone.

detail.abstract: Classical sparse Gaussian mixture detection assumes an exogenous setting in which the probability that a coordinate carries an informative signal is fixed independently of the statistical test. In many settings, however, informative observations must be produced through costly decisions. This paper studies endogenous sparse Gaussian detection, in which privately informed agents strategically decide whether to generate evidence. Capabilities are independent and sparse, with heterogeneous occurrence probabilities. Production costs are private and heterogeneous. A publicly announced test shapes production incentives, so the alternative observation law depends on the resulting equilibrium. Within the Gaussian information feasible region, the main result establishes a sharp information and incentive frontier, Γ * CT (β, r, κ), under a uniform power law comparability condition (CT) on private cost tails. Here β measures capability sparsity, r determines Gaussian signal strength, and κ > 0 describes the abundance of inexpensive producers. The frontier is sharp in the cost exponent γ, which governs the normalized cost scale n-γ : below it, every level-α test admits a low-power independent Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE), while above it, calibrated tests achieve power tending to one at every such equilibrium. The analysis further establishes a sharp three-branch equilibrium frontier for homogeneous deterministic costs. Exact finite-sample equilibrium calculations quantify detection power, evidence production, and the effects of testing rules and private-cost heterogeneity. Monte Carlo simulations independently validate the numerical calculations.

detail.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence can retrieve organizational information, justify recommendations, and invoke enterprise tools, but these capabilities do not automatically confer authority to execute business actions. This conceptual study proposes the Knowledge–Evidence–Authority (KEA) framework to clarify the conditions under which an AI agent's proposed action may be eligible for organizational execution. Drawing on a critical integrative narrative synthesis of knowledge management, evidentiary attribution, organizational decision rights, technical authorization, and AI governance research, KEA distinguishes action-specific Knowledge adequacy (K), Evidentiary integrity (E), and independently enforced Decision authority (A). The framework specifies a non-compensatory policy gate and links the source, warrant, authorization, and disposition records to one agentic action instance. Its main incremental-value proposition is that this linkage may improve audit reconstruction and exception routing compared with otherwise equivalent, independently functioning controls. Five propositions are developed, including a conceptual non-sufficiency rule and an empirical comparative design. Seven illustrative industries—healthcare and pharmaceuticals, insurance, travel and hospitality, consumer packaged goods, banking and finance, telecommunications, and technology—demonstrate how decision contexts alter evidence requirements and permission boundaries without constituting field validation. The paper distinguishes broader governance arrangements from action-specific authority envelopes and identifies important limitations involving policy change, multi-agent handoffs, human oversight, and fairness. KEA is offered as a falsifiable integrative framework, not an empirically validated compliance system or a substitute for existing authorization controls.

detail.abstract: Despite the substantial expansion of banks and financial institutions in Nepal, access to bank credit remains a significant challenge for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). This study examines the firm-level determinants of access to bank credit among Nepalese enterprises, drawing on cross-sectional data from the World Bank Enterprise Survey 2023, comprising 528 firms. Employing a probit regression model, the study estimates marginal effects to assess the influence of various firm-specific characteristics on the likelihood of obtaining bank credit. The explanatory variables include sectoral affiliation, export orientation, auditing practices, and other managerial and firm-level characteristics. The findings highlight the importance of financial transparency and firm productivity in shaping enterprises' access to bank credit. In particular, the results underscore the role of formal auditing practices and productive capacity in strengthening firms' creditworthiness. The study contributes to the empirical literature on SME financing and financial inclusion in developing economies by providing firm-level evidence from Nepal. Its findings offer important policy implications for improving access to formal credit, addressing financing constraints, and promoting a more inclusive and productive private sector.

detail.abstract: In today's digital healthcare environment, ensuring proper execution of rehabilitation exercises remains a major challenge, as traditional home-based therapy often lacks continuous supervision and patients may perform movements incorrectly. The AI-Powered Rehabilitation Coaching System addresses this issue by combining computer vision with biomechanical analysis to assist patients during rehabilitation exercises. The system uses a standard laptop webcam to capture body movements, which are processed using MediaPipe Pose to extract anatomical landmarks. These landmarks are analyzed to calculate joint angles, assess movement patterns, and identify incorrect postures or compensatory movements. An exercise-specific tracking mechanism incorporates filtering and movement validation techniques to improve repetition counting and reduce errors caused by landmark fluctuations. A multi-tier feedback engine provides corrective instructions through visual overlays and voice-based guidance, considering movement deviations and relevant patient conditions. The system also records exercise-session information and generates structured clinical reports containing performance metrics, range of motion measurements, adherence details, and pain assessments. By integrating real-time movement analysis, corrective feedback, and session reporting into a single application, the proposed system aims to support home-based rehabilitation and assist healthcare professionals in monitoring patient exercise performance.

detail.abstract: It is not uncommon for children to be part of social media contents. Some parents post their children's birthdays, achievements, family moments and sometimes even build online audiences around their children, and there is absolutely nothing wrong with this. The problem, however, begins when a child's privacy, dignity, or safety is compromised for views, attention, virtual gifts, or any other form of monetary or material benefit. Nigeria already has laws and policies that protect children from abuse, sexual exploitation and misuse of their personal information. Major online platforms also have systems for detecting, removing and reporting harmful content involving children. The challenge, therefore, is not simply the absence of regulation, but the need for greater public awareness, stronger enforcement, and a better understanding of the responsibilities of parents, platforms, and viewers. This article examines the protections of children from online exploitation already available under Nigerian law, the risks associated with livestreaming and online exposure, and the practical steps to prevent abuse. It also highlights the importance of responsible parenting, prompt reporting, protection of the child's privacy and stronger cooperation between online platforms and Nigerian child-protection authorities.

detail.abstract: We study whether mortgage lenders respond to the threat that generative AI poses to borrowers' earnings by tightening credit. Linking the occupational task exposure of local workforces to generative AI with mortgage applications and labor-market outcomes, we find more permanent layoffs in more-exposed counties, along with higher denial rates on mortgage applications and higher interest rates on originated loans. These credit responses are stronger in metropolitan and high-income areas, in places less susceptible to conventional automation, and among early-career applicants. Denials rise more where task exposure indicates greater scope for labor replacement, and rates rise more where workers face greater obstacles to restoring earnings. Nonbanks respond more strongly than depositories within the same local markets, and lenders originate fewer loans in more-exposed counties, reflecting a contraction in the supply of mortgage credit. Our findings suggest that labor-substituting technology imposes an additional social cost in credit markets, beyond its effects on jobs and wages.

detail.abstract:
This work is the second of two companion studies on the European Federal State (EFS). Report I argued that Europe's crisis is ideological, a mismatch between the national scale at which sovereignty is believed to reside and the continental scale at which it must now be exercised, and that only a federal state limited to five domains can close it. Report II asks whether that state can be built, and how. It sets out the constitutional design: a federation of enumerated competence under a bounded Supremacy Clause, a Federal Chamber and a States Chamber, a parliamentary executive, a Federal Constitutional Court and a justiciable subsidiarity guarantee. It sets out the security order: a Unified Federal Command Structure inside NATO, a single foreign policy decided by majority, a Federal Security Council with a limited emergency power, a federal frontier and asylum system, a federal intelligence agency and a three-stage path for the French deterrent. It sets out the fiscal order: a federal budget of 4.5 percent of GDP, federal bonds, the assumption of legacy debt up to 60 percent of GDP with interest service retained by the states, an automatic stabiliser tested on twenty-five years of data, and the completion of the Banking Union. It then sets out a four-phase transition governed by thresholds rather than dates, including the constitutional routes that Germany, France and the other founding states must take, a timetable of steps, a first-year sequence, and the legal settlement with the Union. Three stress tests and a lawful exit procedure complete the design. The report concludes that the EFS is technically and economically feasible, and that its binding constraint is political will.

detail.abstract: Wildfires pose a severe global threat. In 2025, global wildfires burned approximately 390 million hectares, an area nearly as large as the European Union. This escalating crisis places intense pressure on wildfire management agencies to develop effective strategies to allocate resources. In collaboration with the Government of (redacted for anonymity) , we develop a data-driven framework for day-ahead deployment of suppression resources. Our approach integrates three components: (i) distributional forecasting models that predict daily incident counts and resource-hour requirements under censoring, (ii) a transient analysis of a queueing model that captures short-horizon congestion dynamics, and (iii) a robust optimization model that recommends resource allocations across multiple forest areas under uncertainty. We prove a monotonicity result showing that total expected transient waiting time in an M(t)/E_r/s system is non-decreasing in the arrival rate and mean service time, which yields an exact, tractable reformulation of the robust optimization model as a nominal mixed-integer program. We show that our approach substantially reduces the expected waiting times for wildfires compared to baseline policies. Although our case study focuses on (redacted for anonymity) , the methodology is adaptable and can be tailored to address the challenges of wildfire operations in other regions.

detail.abstract: Public institutions are held to legal standards of efficiency, and employers are held to legal standards of care for the mental health of their workers, yet the two bodies of norms are seldom read together. This article asks at what point, and through which legal instruments, three legal systems bring the human capacity consumed by institutional output into legal account, and whether the decision that sets output expectations falls inside that account. The method is doctrinal and comparative analysis of employer duties in England and Wales (Walker, Hatton, Barber), the European Union and France (Framework Directive 89/391/EEC; Labour Code arts. L4121-1 and L4121-2; the Cour de cassation's decision of 25 November 2015), and Brazil (the constitutional provisions on administrative efficiency and on the reduction of work risks; CNJ Resolution 207/2015; the amended NR-1), complemented by an interpretive reading of the novel O Prédio que Aprendeu a Escutar, used as an analytical case and not as evidence. The thesis is interpretive and normative. Performance targets and risk assessments operate as separate legal instruments, and on the sources verified here none of the regimes examined requires the decision that fixes output expectations to be tested against the human capacity it presupposes. The literatures on the organizational causes of burnout and on employer liability each describe part of the problem but do not join it at the act of target-setting. The article names this gap target-risk decoupling and shows that its consequences differ by regime. It proposes a modest reconciliation duty, an interpretive rule placing target-setting within the organization of work, and paired publication of performance and capacity indicators, and it tests the proposal against the strongest objections, including litigants' interest in speed and the risk that reconciliation becomes one more ritual.

detail.abstract: This paper critically examines how tourism is represented in the Leisure and Tourism sub-strand of Ghana's new Senior High School (SHS) Social Studies curriculum. detail.abstract: Competing market makers must learn quoting strategies from their own trading payoffs while adapting to other makers' behavior. We study this problem in an online market-making game with M makers and K feasible prices. We develop a learning algorithm that combines sequential payoff model alignment with log-barrier regularized best responses. The algorithm uses the structure of market-making payoffs to learn a low-dimensional model for each quote. Equal splitting provides common observations in same-quote experiments, allowing makers to align their local models without communication. The aligned models guide their mixed strategies, while a local regret test determines when to switch to a bandit fallback. We establish two guarantees for the same algorithm. Under our stochastic market model, the terminal mixed-strategy profile has a vanishing Nash gap in self-play. Against nonanticipating opponents, the algorithm achieves O(M√(KT)), up to logarithmic factors, expected maximum pairwise internal regret over T rounds.

detail.abstract:
Goal
This study aims to uncover the fundamental mechanisms driving technological change in complex systems by examining how the evolution of embedded subsystems determines the trajectory and tempo of a host technology.

Background
Building on the theory of technological parasitism, the research conceptualizes modular host systems—such as smartphones—as evolving through dynamic, co‑evolutionary interactions with their constituent subsystems. These interactions transition from parasitic dependence to mutualistic and ultimately symbiotic integration. Central to this theoretical framework is the role of subsystems as temporal pacemakers that influence system‑wide innovation rhythms.

Methods
The study employs a longitudinal, mixed‑methods design, combining an 18‑year case study of the iPhone (2007–2025) with time‑series regression and log‑log hedonic pricing models. The dataset captures performance metrics, subsystem trajectories, and price–performance dynamics across multiple technological generations.

(1) Temporal precedence—Subsystem advances, particularly Bluetooth protocol upgrades, consistently precede host-system releases, with integration lags shrinking from three years to one.
(2) Differential evolutionary pressure—Despite rapid exponential improvement, camera resolution remains a secondary driver of system-level evolution.
(3) Economic pacemakers—Battery life exerts the strongest economic influence, with a 1% performance increase predicting a 0.3% rise in nominal price.

Discussion
These results reveal that subsystems evolve—and influence system trajectories—at different speeds and with unequal systemic leverage. Subsystem evolution acts as a leading indicator of forthcoming architectural transitions.

Implications
The study offers new design rules for forecasting technological generations and informs R&D prioritization by identifying which subsystems function as strategic pacemakers within complex, multi-component innovations.

Originality
This research advances evolutionary theories of modular innovation by demonstrating that complex technologies evolve through asynchronous rhythms among heterogeneous subsystems, establishing subsystem evolution as a governing mechanism of system-level technological change.

detail.abstract:
Why do firms with superior competitive advantage become rigid and exhausted from within, and why do organizations adapting to environmental change face a combinatorial explosion of tactical choices? Static theories of competitive advantage find it difficult to derive self-erosion caused by structural friction endogenously from within the theory, while dynamic adaptation theories lack a mathematical principle for prioritizing interventions.


We propose the Theory of Meta Keystone (TMK), modeling the firm as a non-equilibrium open system on a two-tier coupled network. Extending Strang's equilibrium structure into a two-level variational principle, we couple a lower-tier operational flow network with an upper-tier cellular sheaf representing inter-unit translation of meanings, rules, and control signals. Upper-tier interpretive and institutional twists (sheaf curvature) and rework loops driven by queueing backpressure (curl-field vortices in the discrete Hodge-Helmholtz decomposition) endogenously contract effective operational capacity. Three core results emerge. First, under quotient-graph coarse-graining, throughput is governed scale-invariantly by the minimum cut (the keystone), where non-bottleneck investments yield zero direct first-order sensitivity, drastically compressing the tactical search space. Second, orthogonal Hodge decomposition separates productive baseline flow and governance-sustaining harmonic circulation from unproductive rework vortices, explaining employee burnout and sublinear scaling amid chronic busyness. Third, overcoming capacity degradation requires rewiring network topology and flattening sheaf friction; however, unlike physical Constructal transport networks under restricted conditions, the sheaf Laplacian's spectral gap, conformity coupling, and local bistable pinning create a positive Dirichlet energy barrier that impedes sub-critical uniform top-down mandates and manifests financially as SG&A cost stickiness, positioning local nucleation as a viable pathway for transformation.


We operationalize TMK via the LESS Loop protocol, the Time Conversion Ratio (TCR), a nine-indicator early-warning system, and a 25-year comparative analysis of Boeing and Airbus.

detail.abstract: This study examines the long-term association between childhood malnutrition and youth economic exclusion in Africa using a 20-year lagged country-level panel analysis. Specifically, it investigates whether childhood stunting, measured through the prevalence of stunting among children under five during 2000-2004, is statistically associated with youth not in employment, education or training (NEET) rates during 2020-2024. The analysis combines country-level data and employs pooled ordinary least squares (OLS) and country fixed-effects estimators, progressively incorporating controls for baseline GDP per capita, population growth, urbanisation and government effectiveness. The pooled OLS estimates initially indicate a negative and statistically significant association between childhood stunting and subsequent youth NEET rates. However, this relationship becomes statistically insignificant after accounting for country characteristics. In the fully controlled fixed-effects specification, the estimated coefficient is approximately zero and statistically insignificant (β =-0.0004, p = 0.996). These findings suggest that the initial negative association does not provide robust evidence of a long-term statistical relationship between childhood stunting and youth economic exclusion across African countries. The study highlights the importance of accounting for country-level heterogeneity when investigating long-term relationships between early-life conditions and subsequent socioeconomic outcomes.

detail.abstract: The productivity gains from AI often depend on knowledge held by the workers it may replace. Sharing this knowledge can improve workers' productivity while making them easier to replace, giving them an incentive to withhold it. We study a two-period model in which a worker teaches a firm-owned AI, but the firm cannot commit to future employment or compensation. We characterize optimal severance contracts and show that full teaching may be impossible to implement. A regulator that maximizes the worker's payoff can resolve this problem through a dismissal tax transferred to the worker. Despite its inability to commit to future policies, worker-optimal regulation implements efficient teaching and employment. We also examine the effects of commitment to future severance and the presence of a second worker.

detail.abstract: Internet shutdowns have spread worldwide and are usually understood as repression: governments cut connectivity to silence critics and demobilize protest. I show that in India, which accounts for 44 percent of documented shutdowns, deployment follows a logic of selective protection: orders answer violence that threatens communities whose votes the government needs. detail.abstract: Egypt's Universal Health Insurance (UHI) system, established by Law No. 2 of 2018, is the state's flagship instrument for delivering Egypt Vision 2030's commitment to accessible, quality healthcare for every citizen. Phase one is complete in six governorates, and phase two — led by Minya and covering more than 12 million people — is now under way. In October 2026 a Prime Ministerial committee set the direction clearly: plan for completion within no more than ten years and cover 50% of the population by 2030. Accelerating coverage at this pace is not only a question of hospitals and enrolment; it is a question of medicines. Every new beneficiary becomes a prescription that must be forecast, procured, priced, manufactured and dispensed. Egypt has strong foundations: a WHO Maturity Level 3 regulator, local production that meets about 91% of medicine needs, a single public bulk purchaser, and more than 81 million electronic prescriptions inside UHI itself. This policy brief argues that the speed of UHI will increasingly be set by the medicines value chain. It proposes five practical, low-cost measures: a national UHI Medicines Intelligence Platform that links existing data into one forecasting layer; a standard Medicine Readiness Study before each governorate enters the system; multi-year, volume-based "local-first" framework agreements to support manufacturing and API localisation; an institutionalised health technology assessment and managed-entry pathway for high-cost medicines; and a last-mile pharmacy access network, starting in Minya. The recommendations require coordination more than new spending, and each can be piloted within the current legal framework.

detail.abstract: Delegating resume screening to large language models (LLMs) requires organizations to establish whether they can distinguish candidates by relevant qualifications while allowing only authorized users to change screening rules or approve exceptions. To this end, we develop a system architecture that separates candidate evidence, evaluation, permission controls, and assessment record, and empirically examine two complementary dimensions of its deployment readiness. First, we assess its operational readiness on four LLMs using a controlled experiment on 210 resumes across 14 job roles and six decision interfaces. Second, we assess its compliance readiness by testing how it handles unauthorized user requests and instructions embedded in resumes. We find that operational performance depends on the choice of evaluation interface: scalar scores generally distinguish qualification changes better than simple pass/fail judgments, while comparative judgments are sensitive to presentation order. Explicit permission rules and separation of resume content from instructions reduce unauthorized compliance, to a varying degree of effectiveness across LLMs and usage contexts. Finally, we find that LLM evaluators often diverge between their decisions and offered justifications. Going beyond simply evaluating LLMs for hiring tasks, our framework supports an audit of a fully configured resume evaluation system to enable its deployment decision.

detail.abstract: This paper examines Albania’s judicial vetting (2016–2024) as an extraordinary accountability mechanism, analysing results from 805 vetted magistrates using operational judicial data. Despite achieving comprehensive personnel transformation (47% magistrate removal norm)1 validated by European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) in 98.9% of cases, three critical dynamics challenged Albanian vetting design: (1) institutional resistance through strategic utilization of legal mechanisms, including 113 resignations that maintain the eligibility of re-appointment after the 15-year ban expires in 2032; (2) operational trade-offs as personnel reduction has dropped judicial capacity to its lowest level by 54%; (3) sustainability gaps as vetting transitional frameworks lacked continuity provisions for the transfer of vetting standards into permanent accountability institutions (HJC and HPC) before vetting bodies mandate expiration in 2026. These dynamics led to the creation of an accountability gap, demonstrated by only a 1.1% conviction rate of vetted magistrates, time-barred cases, coordination failures, evidentiary gaps, resource constraints, and a decline in public trust. Despite structural limitations of vetting design that prioritize short-term transformation over sustainable judicial accountability, overall Albania’s vetting has disrupted past entrenched impunity patterns. For transitional societies, the lesson for vetting design is to ensure institutionalized accountability mechanisms in permanent institutions by simultaneously preserving the judicial capacity

detail.abstract: Electronic design automation (EDA) software and third-party semiconductor intellectual property (IP) are licensed, not sold. They reach licensees as a stream of updates, license keys, support, and design data that crosses borders for years, and they end up embedded in chips made and sold worldwide. Since 2020, U.S. export controls on chip design have changed repeatedly, through a foreign direct product rule aimed at chip designs made with U.S. tools, an end use control on the design of advanced-node chips, a rule treating software license keys as the software they unlock, license requirements imposed on EDA vendors by letter in May 2025 and rescinded in July 2025, and a rule extending Entity List restrictions to affiliates owned 50 percent or more by listed entities, which was stayed six weeks after it took effect and, on the day the stay was due to end, stayed again until January 2027. In settlements reached in 2025 and 2026, the Bureau of Industry and Security treated downloads and automatic updates delivered to listed customers and end users as unlicensed exports. The contracts that carry these products were not written for this pace of change. Their export clauses tend to restate the duty to comply with the law and say little about what happens to fees, users, keys, and design data when the law changes in the middle of the term. This Article argues that the allocation of export control risk in chip design licenses should move from generic compliance boilerplate to a public, modular set of default clauses built on information forcing, proportional suspension, and reversible remedies. It develops such clauses, released separately as an open consultation draft under the name Chip Design Export Clauses, and maps each clause to the provision of the Export Administration Regulations that it serves. It also acknowledges the limits of private ordering, because a contract cannot change who is liable to the government. detail.abstract: In this paper, we examine how the charitable safety net responds to state caps of 36 percent on the annual percentage rate of small dollar loans. The funding expansion extends to sectors that do not serve payday borrowers, whereas reallocation toward individual assistance is statistically significant only in the NPOs that serve credit constrained households. Our results suggest that rate caps and the public funding expansion reflect a shared electoral preference for redistribution. The findings link small dollar credit regulation to the funding and activities of the charitable safety net.

title: SOUL-E (Self-Optimizing Universal Learner – Engine): Preliminary Results Show Its Models Outperform Time-series Foundation Models and Gradient-Boosted Trees on Unseen Data in a Pre-Registered Comparison of One-Day-Ahead Stock and Cryptocurrency Ranking

detail.title: SOUL-E (Self-Optimizing Universal Learner – Engine): Preliminary Results Show Its Models Outperform Time-series Foundation Models and Gradient-Boosted Trees on Unseen Data in a Pre-Registered Comparison of One-Day-Ahead Stock and Cryptocurrency Ranking

declarations.declarationOfInterest: M.J.T.V. and Y.J.K. are affiliated with CyAura, which develops SOUL-E. The results are historical simulations tested on unseen data in different market regimes, not live trading, and do not constitute investment advice. Names of third-party models and companies are used for identification only.

detail.abstract: Whether time-series foundation models rank financial assets reliably on unseen data is underexplored, and AI systems that design AI models remain immature where high precision is required. We report a pre-registered comparison of oneday-ahead ranking of 100 S&P 500 stocks and 50 crypto assets, in which every model family is selected in advance by one rule and scored on unseen data: three segments on which no compared model was trained, tuned or selected, one of them prospective, made of data that did not exist when the unseen windows were fixed. Benchmarks are 32 configurations of TimesFM 2.5 (Google Research), Chronos-2 and Chronos-Bolt (Amazon), Moirai 2.0 (Salesforce), Toto 2.0 (Datadog), TiRex-2 (NXAI) and AutoGluon-TimeSeries (Amazon), 12 of LightGBM (Microsoft), CatBoost (Yandex) and XGBoost (DMLC), and short-term reversal, compared with CyAura V0.2, the current model of SOUL-E, a machine-learning factory that automates the design, training, validation and evolution of forecasting architectures. On unseen data, CyAura V0.2 reached a mean daily rank information coefficient (IC) of 0.089 on stocks and 0.084 on crypto, 1.9 and 2.4 times the best of the 44 and 43 external configurations identified with hindsight on the same data (0.047 and 0.035); it exceeded every one of them and short-term reversal, with all paired differences excluding zero under two block bootstraps. It kept 89% (stocks) and 91% (crypto) of its IC on the pseudo-out-of-sample test period, against 61% and 63% for the best foundation-model/AutoML configuration chosen with hindsight; of the other families, only the best stock LightGBM/CatBoost configuration held its level (0.041 to 0.047), about half that of CyAura V0.2. Its IC contribution was positive for 86 of 100 stocks and 44 of 50 crypto assets (comparators: at most 72 and 33), and it met the pre-registered endpoints on the confirmatory sample (Benjamini-Yekutieli q = 0.007 and q < 0.0001). For portfolio use, the top tenth of its stock ranking beat the bottom tenth by 56.5 basis points a day (t = 6.9); neutralized against six standard price exposures, short-term reversal among them, it kept 66% and 61% of its IC, against at most 0.017 and 0.020 for the benchmarks selected in advance or with hindsight; and added with equal weight to a price-factor composite, it raised the composite's IC from 0.039 to 0.075 (stocks) and from 0.055 to 0.080 (crypto). The stock ranking must be executed at the close and is renewed almost entirely each day. Its final models trained in 5.16 hours on a laptop processor, and SOUL-E's logged search took about 129 consumer machine-hours, partly estimated.

detail.abstract:
Purpose-This paper aims to specifically focus on the challenges that human resource management (HRM) leaders and departments in contemporary organisations face due to close interaction between artificial intelligence (AI) (primarily robots) and human workers especially at the team level. It further discusses important potential strategies, which can be useful to overcome these challenges based on a conceptual review of extant research. 

Design/methodology/approach-The current paper undertakes a conceptual work where multiple streams of literature are integrated to present a rather holistic yet critical overview of the relationship between AI (particularly robots) and HRM in contemporary organisations. 

Findings-We highlight that interaction and collaboration between human workers and robots is visible in a range of industries and organisational functions, where both are working as team members. This gives rise to unique challenges for HRM function in contemporary organisations where they need to address workers' fear of working with AI, especially in relation to future job loss and difficult dynamics associated with building trust between human workers and AI-enabled robots as team members. Along with these, human workers' task fulfilment expectations with their AI-enabled robot colleagues need to be carefully communicated and managed by HRM staff to maintain the collaborative spirit, as well as future performance evaluations of employees. The authors found that organisational support mechanisms such as facilitating environment, training opportunities and ensuring a viable technological competence level before organising human workers in teams with robots are important. Finally, we found that one of the toughest challenges for HRM relates to performance evaluation in teams where both humans and AI (including robots) work side by side. We referred to the lack of existing frameworks to guide HRM managers in this concern and stressed the possibility of taking insights from the computer gaming literature, where performance evaluation models have been developed to analyse humans and AI interactions while keeping the context and limitations of both in view.

Originality/value-Our paper is one of the few studies that go beyond a rather general or functional analysis of AI in the HRM context. It specifically focusses on the teamwork dimension, where human workers and AI-powered machines (robots) work together and offer insights and suggestions for such teams' smooth functioning.

detail.abstract: This paper focuses on an under-researched topic of knowledge sharing dynamics in international subcontracting relationships of SMEs. Based on in-depth qualitative analysis of three Finnish high-tech firms, our findings reveal that not only cost and performance expectations motivate SMEs for international subcontracting, but also the factors like lack of in-house alternatives, the volatility of workload, and need for speed in growth-related activities such as deliveries play an important role. We further found that the SMEs try to balance internal risks/uncertainty and external risks/uncertainty throughout international subcontracting. Our paper contributes to the extant literature by being one of the first studies to specifically highlight the range of knowledge sharing and knowledge protection mechanisms used in international subcontracting in SME-SME relationships in which partners come from different institutional settings and physical locations. Moreover, this paper is one of the few studies to specifically highlight the role of time in knowledge sharing from the buyer's point of view as well, specifically by emphasizing the need to balance the internal and external risks during the life-cycle of international subcontracting while balancing short-term challenges and long-term strategic development plans. The full paper is available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.intman.2021.100888

title: Policy Design That Does Not Require Heroes: When Should Policy Change Constraints Rather Than People? Min-won Lee

detail.title: Policy Design That Does Not Require Heroes: When Should Policy Change Constraints Rather Than People? Min-won Lee

declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: When people do not behave as a policy expects, analysts tend to explain the gap by attitudes: weak civic spirit, low commitment to place, bureaucratic self-interest. This article argues that such explanations often end causal inquiry too early. It proposes the ordinary-human principle: before attributing unexpected behavior to the attitudes of the people who display it, researchers should ask why that behavior is advantageous under the constraints those people face, and whether a feasible policy could make the desired behavior less costly. The ordinary person is neither the knight nor the knave of earlier policy theory. She is reasonably rational, modestly public-spirited, and unwilling to bear extraordinary personal sacrifice. The article makes three contributions. First, it defines required-action compensation, the burden a policy imposes when it asks for behavior that differs from what a person would choose under existing conditions. Second, it extends the principle along the whole policy chain, from targets and stakeholders to policymakers, frontline implementers, and the researchers who propose and evaluate policy, and states a single condition under which the chain carries a policy as intended. Third, it derives testable propositions about when policy should change constraints rather than people, together with a constraint-response test that makes structural explanations falsifiable. An application to public institutions relocated out of Seoul illustrates how the principle changes research questions and conclusions.

detail.abstract: High-dimensional portfolio optimization is frequently constrained by the curse of dimensionality and liquidity traps, as traditional frameworks assume homogeneous liquidity and static correlations. To address this, this study proposes a robust portfolio optimization framework grounded in a liquidity stratification network. First, a dual-dimensional metric combining the Amihud illiquidity ratio and average daily volume dynamically classifies assets into core, edge, and zombie tiers. A graph attention network then captures asymmetric liquidity risk transmission, generating a dynamic similarity matrix that drives a liquidity-adjusted hierarchical risk parity model for recursive risk budgeting. To adapt to non-stationary markets, a macro-state perception module translates economic cycle signals into state-dependent position bounds and turnover constraints. The resulting high-dimensional non-convex optimization is solved via a three-stage serial meta-heuristic solver—integrating covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy, adaptive differential evolution, and parallel simulated annealing—initialized with a structural warm-start prior. An out-of-sample backtest spanning 255 trading weeks (October 2020 to September 2025) demonstrates that the strategy achieves a cumulative return of 298.90% and an annualized return of 32.60%, with 19.63% volatility and a 1.5298 Sharpe ratio. The maximum drawdown is strictly contained at -21.00%. Crucially, the framework maintains practical executability, yielding an 8.54% weekly turnover and cumulative transaction costs of only 3.75% of initial capital. Statistical tests and bootstrap confidence intervals further validate the robustness of risk-adjusted returns. Sensitivity analyses, ablation experiments, and benchmark comparisons confirm the model significantly outperforms conventional methods in post-cost performance and microstructure feasibility. By endogenizing liquidity heterogeneity, this research bridges the gap between theoretical construction and actual trading frictions, offering institutional investors a rigorous, implementable allocation paradigm for complex macroeconomic regimes.

detail.abstract: Cultural Capital shapes negotiation outcomes and power dynamics, yet remains largely overlooked in Foreign Direct Investments (FDI) to Sri Lanka’s energy sector. FDI is often assessed through economic, political, and strategic frameworks, but attention to socio-cultural dimensions highlights how cultural capital shapes investment outcomes and policy responses. The study examines how Chinese and Indian investors use cultural capital to build influence in Sri Lanka’s energy sector and how policymakers and local stakeholders perceive these investments. Drawing on Pierre Bourdieu’s theory of cultural capital, the study adopts qualitative methods, including document analysis and interviews, and reveals that investments from India and China deploy embodied, objectified, and institutionalized cultural capital to influence deals, legitimize authority, and reproduce dependency. Sri Lankan government negotiators, however, often overlook this form of capital contributing to weakened bargaining positions. Key findings highlight investors' strategic use of cultural capital to soften resistance, reinforce technocratic hierarchies, and maintain dependence on foreign expertise and infrastructure systems. Chinese investments displayed reliance on commercialized rapid infrastructure delivery and objectified cultural capital, particularly in fossil fuel and large-scale infrastructure projects. Indian investments emphasized more tailored institutionalized cultural capital through policy alignment, training programs, regional energy integration, and diplomatic agreements. The study also identifies significant governance gaps within Sri Lanka’s energy sector, including fragmented institutional coordination, limited project literacy, reactive policymaking, and unequal negotiation power. Although the official memoranda and joint statements framed the partnerships as mutually beneficial, the negotiation processes reflected asymmetrical power relations shaped by investor country self-interests and symbolic authority. The significance of the research lies in the study's contribution to improving Sri Lanka’s agency in future energy negotiations by identifying weaknesses in domestic institutional coordination, technical literacy, and diplomacy. The study positions cultural capital as an underexplored factor in understanding contemporary energy governance, foreign influence, and dependency in developing states.

title: Capacity, Not Commitment: Administrative Capacity Deficits and the Statutory Deferral of the EU AI Act

detail.title: Capacity, Not Commitment: Administrative Capacity Deficits and the Statutory Deferral of the EU AI Act

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: Funder statement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: On 2 August 2026, the core obligations governing high-risk artificial intelligence systems under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 were due to become applicable. They did not. Six days before that date, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744-the Digital Omnibus on AI-entered into force, deferring the stand-alone high-risk regime to 2 December 2027 and the embedded-product regime to 2 August 2028. The dominant reading of this deferral treats it as deregulatory retreat: a European Union bending to industrial pressure and a competitiveness agenda. This article advances an alternative and, it argues, better-supported explanation. The deferral is more accurately understood as a revealed administrative capacity deficit. Its proximate cause, stated in the operative recitals of the amending Regulation itself, was the delayed availability of harmonised standards and the failure of a substantial share of Member States to designate and empower the national competent authorities on which the entire enforcement architecture dependsa designation obligation that fell due on 2 August 2025 and that, ten months later, remained unfulfilled across two-thirds of the Union. Drawing on Lodge and Wegrich's typology of administrative capacities and on the management school of compliance theory, the article characterises the AI Act as a capacity-blind statute: an instrument that specifies regulatory outputs in considerable detail while treating the administrative capability required to produce them as exogenous and assured. It substantiates this claim through a structured comparison of four Member State administrations-Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands and Estonia-and then demonstrates, through the parallel cases of the Digital Services Act and the General Data Protection Regulation, that the defect is recurrent rather than incidental. The article concludes by specifying four elements of capacity-sensitive regulatory design, of which conditional commencement is the most consequential. The contribution is to relocate the analysis of EU digital regulation from the question of what the Union legislates to the question of whether its Member States can administer what it legislates.

title: Calibration of US Election Markets: Primaries versus General Elections on Kalshi and Polymarket, with a Pre-Registered Test on the 2026 Midterms

detail.title: Calibration of US Election Markets: Primaries versus General Elections on Kalshi and Polymarket, with a Pre-Registered Test on the 2026 Midterms

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I am not sponsored by neither Kalshi nor Polymarket, and I have no affiliation with either organisation. My analysis is numerical and unbiased.
declarations.funderStatement: Myself

detail.abstract: Betting markets are known to underprice favourites. The favourite-longshot bias first documented at racetracks also appears on Kalshi and Polymarket, where political markets look slightly underconfident. We ask whether this holds equally for primaries and general elections. Using every two-candidate US contest settled on the two platforms between November 2023 and September 2026, priced at a fixed time on election day before polls close, we fit one number, a stretch, that measures whether favourites win more often (above 1) or less often (below 1) than their prices imply. General elections followed the familiar pattern (5 November 2024: 1.97 on Kalshi, 1.83 on Polymarket), but Kalshi primaries went the other way, with favourites winning far less often than priced (0.32); Polymarket's primaries were close to calibrated. Because most general elections in the data were from 2024 and most primaries from 2026, the split could mean either that primaries are traded differently or that the underconfidence faded over time. The midterms provide a prospective test of whether general-election underconfidence remains detectable in 2026. We pre-registered that test, archived it before the US midterms of 3 November 2026, and ran it on those general elections. In this preliminary run (187 contests on Kalshi, 145 on Polymarket; 40 still unsettled), Polymarket remained underconfident (1.66, 95% interval 1.21 to 2.91) and consistent with 2024: evidence against the underconfidence simply fading, though not proof that the type of election explains the contrast. Kalshi's result (1.32, 0.88 to 2.35) was inconclusive, although on the 141 races both platforms listed, both were underconfident to the same degree. Buying favourites priced above 70% earned a few percent per bet after costs, but two general-election nights cannot show whether the bias can be traded. A final version will follow once every contest has settled.

detail.abstract: Negotiation is one of the most common forms of social interaction and conflict resolution strategies-occurring in business, workplaces, and organizations-in which two or more parties strive to figure out an acceptable solution for their different or incompatible goals. These complex bargaining processes are always characterized by various psychological aspects. This article sheds light on two significant cognitive components impacting all facets and stages of negotiation-egocentrism and self-serving bias. Their negative effects on negotiation regarding fairness judgment, information distortion, and interactional dynamics are presented, explained, and illustrated. The paper addresses how egocentric perceptions and self-serving tendencies affect the ethical behavior of the involved parties, and it looks at these biases through intercultural lens too. The article concludes by proposing tactics and practices aimed to reduce the damaging consequences of egocentric shortcomings in negotiation and increase chances to achieve the best possible outcomes.

detail.abstract: ehubX is an open-source Python framework for the optimization-based planning of multi-energy systems, from buildings and districts to regions and countries. Users describe demands, candidate technologies such as heat pumps, photovoltaics, wind turbines, batteries and aquifer thermal energy storage, networks, and energy imports with prices and emissions in YAML and CSV files. ehubX then determines which technologies to install, when, at what capacity, and how to operate them to minimize cost or net CO 2 emissions, to maximize self-sufficiency, or to trade off two of these objectives. By default, it formulates a mixed-integer linear program that is solved by an external solver. Energy carriers and materials such as CO 2 are balanced as commodities, so that carbon capture, utilization and storage is planned together with the energy supply. Networks of interconnected sites, multi-stage pathways and time-series aggregation that retains seasonal storage are supported.

detail.abstract: African governments rely heavily on commodity exports for fiscal revenue and spend heavily on commodity imports. Standard analyses summarize this exposure through the terms of trade: when export prices fall or import prices rise, the ratio deteriorates and debt increases. But export and import prices often fall simultaneously. I show that this common decline raises sovereign debt even though the terms of trade is unchanged. Using separately identified export and import price shocks for twenty African economies over 1990-2019, I find that a 10 percent export-price decline raises sovereign debt by 5.7 percentage points of GDP after four years; an equal import-price increase lowers it by 3.4 points; and a simultaneous 10 percent decline in both raises it by 6 points. Export-price shocks reduce government revenue with a delay, as commodity receipts take time to reach the budget; import-price increases lower debt largely through the GDP deflator: higher import prices raise the price level, expanding nominal GDP and reducing the debt ratio. Frameworks that summarize external price exposure through relative prices or one price at a time miss the debt that accumulates when both fall together, understating sovereign fiscal risk.

detail.abstract: South Africa's electricity utility, Eskom, and its municipal customers face large non-payment, but little is known about how much of it reflects inability rather than unwillingness to pay. This paper combines the General Household Survey 2025, the Income and Expenditure Survey 2022/23 and municipal indigent registers to estimate how many households do not pay, how many could afford a bill, and what recovering their payments would mean for revenue. About 2.67 million households (14.7% of those answering) report not paying. Because the two surveys cannot be linked at household level, I bound the number able to pay under three assumptions about who the non-payers are. With a threshold of 10% of income, between 1.35 and 2.63 million non-paying households could afford a bill, with a middle case of 2.17 million. At 2025/26 prices, collecting from households that can afford to pay would add roughly R5 to R11 billion a year, 1.4% to 2.9% of Eskom's allowable revenue, about half of it reaching Eskom directly, and would lower the price implied for other customers by a few percent at most. About 18.4% of households with a bill spend at least 10% of income on electricity, and half would do so at a real price about 2.6 times the 2022/23 level if consumption were unchanged. The results are stable across robustness checks. They are preliminary: survey years differ, several inputs are scenario assumptions, and some reported figures await verification. detail.abstract: Machine learning can identify suspicious cloud activity at volumes that exceed manual review capacity. Its operational value depends on how well a detection policy handles rare incidents, incomplete audit evidence and differences in the consequences of compromise. This study combines a targeted synthesis of intrusion detection, model calibration and cloud audit research with a deterministic sensitivity analysis at the candidate-case level. Four models quantify alert precision under changing incident prevalence, review demand under a finite analyst budget, the conditions under which a high-impact case should outrank a higher-probability case, and the effects of unequal evidence coverage on incident recovery. In a worked scenario of 100,000 candidate cases, 0.05% incident prevalence and 80% recall, a 0.1% false-positive rate produces about 140 alerts and 28.6% precision. A capacity of 100 reviews limits the feasible false-positive rate to approximately 0.0600% at the same recall. When incident observability falls from 90% to 50%, end-to-end recall falls from 72% to 40% with conditional recall fixed at 80%. These results arise from stated assumptions and can be reproduced directly from the equations. They motivate an evaluation protocol that joins chronological and account-held-out tests with evidence coverage, analyst workload and calibration checks. The study identifies which quantities a cloud security team must estimate before using machine learning scores to allocate response capacity. AI disclosure. detail.abstract: Many software development organizations have replaced traditional project-oriented work and maintenance teams with persistent, cross-functional, and autonomous product teams. The claimed benefits are said to affect the full life cycle of software systems, particularly regarding the value creation related to the product or service they aim to support. However, the supporting evidence is sparse. We report on a survey of 60 experienced practitioners, each describing an IT system they know well, in which we assessed product orientation in both the original development phase and in present-day work. In addition, respondents selected the lifetime cost, benefit, and technical debt trajectory they believed would best match their IT system. We find that product orientation has increased from the development phase to today and that higher product orientation at development is associated with better productivity and technical quality, as perceived by the respondents. Higher present-day product orientation is associated with more favorable benefit and technical debt life-cycle trajectories, while the association with the life-cycle cost trajectories is weak and partly confounded by system age. We discuss implications of the findings, along with limitations of the study design.

detail.abstract: A construction team may have to act on a change while its price, schedule implications and contractual basis are still under review. This study examines how teams can make that decision without losing track of what was authorised, what was built and what should be paid. An integrative review of construction change, rework, procurement and financial control informs the proposed framework. The study also analyses 52 New York City agency-level records for fiscal years 2018 through 2020, covering 3,580 construction and 266 design change orders. These records describe the volume, recorded value and processing time of reported orders. A separate exercise compares immediate release, waiting for verification and releasing a limited portion of the work across 225 hypothetical scenarios. The least-cost response depends on the exposure from proceeding, the cost of waiting and the expense of staging the work. The framework carries the evidence behind each decision through valuation, certification and payment. It distinguishes legitimate scope growth, outstanding exposure and the costs attributable to avoidable errors or delays. detail.abstract: This paper investigates the efficiency effects of governing vertical relationships by analyzing the incentives of firms to engage in exclusive contracts. When a downstream firm possesses a superior bargaining position, upstream subcontractors do not prefer an exclusive contract, even when it is efficient, as such a contract lowers their bargaining power even further, ultimately leading to lower profits. detail.abstract: This study examines the long-term effects of higher national debt in South Korea on asset distribution. Using an overlapping generations general equilibrium model, we focus on two key channels: rising interest rates and falling wage rates, both driven by the crowding-out effect of capital. Higher interest rates increase asset dispersion, benefiting older groups with more accumulated assets, while younger groups with fewer assets gain less. Falling wage rates reduce the capacity to save money across all age groups, partially offsetting the dispersion effects of higher interest rates. A simulation of a 50% increase in national debt reveals a decline in the Gini coefficient of asset holdings, driven by the diminishing marginal increase in future assets relative to current holdings. However, widening cross-sectional dispersion proved more welfare-relevant: older age groups, which experienced greater gains in average assets, saw increases in average welfare, whereas early life-cycle cohorts with low asset levels experienced welfare losses. Given this trade-off associated with higher national debt, initial asset transfers as a counteracting measure can enhance lifetime welfare overall, mitigate the rising asset dispersion, and improve the asset Gini coefficient.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how government venture capital (GVC) affects firm growth and financing in small and medium-sized enterprises. Using matched panel data for Swedish firms over 2008-2020, we evaluate impacts on employment, sales, equity, and debt. GVC-backed firms expand employment almost immediately after investment, while sales growth follows with a lag of two to three years. GVC participation also strengthens firms' equity positions and improves access to bank credit, consistent with certification and balance-sheet channels that alleviate financial constraints. Importantly, the positive impacts are concentrated in metropolitan and innovation-dense regions. Despite receiving a disproportionately large share of GVC funding due to regional allocation rules, rural and peripheral regions display notably weaker effects, suggesting that local ecosystem depth moderates program effectiveness. These findings highlight the dual role of GVC as both growth finance and a mechanism for reducing capital-market imperfections, while raising policy questions about the efficiency of geographically earmarked allocation. These findings demonstrate that GVC generates genuine financial additionality by improving both equity and credit access. detail.abstract: The Mississippi River offers cost and environmental advantages for freight; however, containerized service remains underused. This paper presents a prefeasibility market screening framework for a hypothetical container-on-barge service at 15 Mississippi mainstem candidate nodes, using 9,797,087 import records across 12 consignee states. detail.abstract: Anti-money laundering (AML) increasingly relies on artificial intelligence, yet the humans who use these systems, oversee them, and answer for them in court often cannot see why a system flagged a given transaction. We ask whether and how explainable AI (XAI) can close this gap for banks and other obliged entities, financial intelligence units (FIUs), and supervisory authorities. We combine legal and technical analysis with three exploratory expert interviews. The analysis distinguishes between two kinds of explainability: operational, which helps analysts at obliged entities and FIUs validate models and handle cases, and post-operational, which allows supervisors and judges to scrutinize decisions after the fact. The institutional value of an AI explanation depends on the reference data and feature dependencies built into the system, and on how users interpret and challenge what they are shown. Explanations can aid investigation and improve models, but they can also encourage confirmation bias, misplaced reliance, and cognitive overload. We therefore argue that the explainability requirements of the EU AI Act, data protection law, and the AML framework must be implemented through governance. Institutions should preserve explanations that can be reproduced, document the reasoning of human reviewers, and allow decisions to be meaningfully contested. We outline the complementary roles of the EU Anti-Money Laundering Authority and the courts in setting these standards. Humans and machines can complement one another in AML when explanations begin scrutiny and form a necessary starting point for fostering legal judgment.

detail.abstract: AML supervision and enforcement relies to a large extent on the analytical power of Financial Intelligence Units (FIUs) that receive suspicious transaction or activity reports (STRs/SARs) and pass them on to law enforcement authorities. This paper analyses their role under the EU regulatory status quo and how it will change under the new AML framework. By combining comparative legal and descriptive empirical approaches based on numbers extracted from FIUs' annual reports, it shows the current heterogeneity of European FIUs when it comes to their organisational setup, staffing, STR exposure, and interaction via information requests. detail.abstract: People who share the same context and the same information often reach different understandings. This paper proposes the Object Perspective Principle as one explanation. The principle states that context supplies content, and that the object on which attention is concentrated supplies the perspective from which that content is read. Understanding needs both. I define four terms (context, content, object, and perspective) so that each can be identified separately, and I treat understanding as the outcome. I then extend the principle in three directions. First, an object can be chosen by the person or imposed by a situation, a role, a crisis, or another person, and an imposed object can be examined and reframed. Second, when several objects are held together, each one acts on perspective, and the dominant object decides the understanding. Third, the principle applies to individuals, teams, and organisations, where only the source of the object changes. I place the principle beside research on attention, framing, sensemaking, goals, and the attention based view of the firm, and I state where it agrees with that work and what it adds. Ten testable propositions and a first experimental study are set out. This is a conceptual working paper. The propositions are open for empirical testing.

detail.abstract: Fast-fashion and commercial apparel studios increasingly sample and approve surface prints on high-speed digital inkjet plotters, which offer short setup times, seamless repeat proofs, and multi-ink process colour with fine droplet placement. Approval, however, is not production. When an approved design is scaled to a rotary screen line, the print must be re-expressed in a different colourant system, a different colour-building logic, and a different physical constraint set: engraved screens, a bounded number of colour stations, repeat dimensions tied to screen circumference, and paste-based fixation and wash-off. This paper argues that the interval between digital approval and a stable rotary run is a distinct and under-governed handoff, and that it concentrates three costs that are rarely accounted for together: colour-matching latency, screen calibration iterations, and machine idle time. We frame these as articulation work in Strauss's and Star's sense, the invisible coordination that reconciles an approved design with the contingent reality of production, and as a bottleneck problem in the sense of the Theory of Constraints. We propose a five-gate operational protocol that places explicit decisions at print-feasibility screening, colour translation, screen release, on-press calibration, and run release, and we outline a qualitative, mixed-evidence study design combining 8 to 12 practitioner interviews with process mapping of recent scale-up cases to locate and, where records permit, quantify these delays. We position this as a workshop paper and open preprint intended to seed a larger empirical study, not as a completed empirical investigation.

detail.abstract: Across ultra-large-scale manufacturing networks, smart power grids, global logistics corridors, and national resource allocation systems-all prime examples of Open Complex Giant Systems (OCGS)-computer science and Operations Research (OR) have long confronted a seemingly insurmountable mathematical barrier: Combinatorial Explosion (the NP-Hard curse). When system scale expands to 500,000 demand orders, a 20-level Bill of Materials (20-level BOM), and 2,000,000 material items, conventional Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) solvers and commercial Advanced Planning and Scheduling (APS) packages routinely suffer multi-hour runtime timeouts or memory exhaustion. Simultaneously, in engineering implementation, industry practice overwhelmingly favors a purely "Top-Down" construction sequence-erecting monthly executive dashboards (S&OP/IBP) first while leaving daily shop-floor execution to manual spreadsheetscausing top-level plans to decouple from shop-floor reality. Grounded in Value Chain Physics and first principles of complex systems, this paper formulates and proves the physical computation and engineering construction law that pierces combinatorial explosion: The Law of Orthogonal Pruning. First, we prove that conventional mathematical programming encounters factorial 𝒪(𝑁!) combinatorial explosion because uniform algebraic symbols obliterate the boundary between two physically opposite quantities in a controlled network: Extensive Flows (such as multi-period material kitting flows, which obey quantity additivity and inter-temporal flow conservation) and Intensive/Discrete Capacities (such as bottleneck machine time slots, which possess strict spatiotemporal exclusivity and cannot be accumulated across periods), mixing both into a single monolithic matrix for coupled search. Second, by orthogonally separating these two physical classes-Stage 1 executes network-wide parallel water-level pulling on Extensive Flows along true multi-echelon kitting bottleneck dates in linear time 𝒪(𝑁), pruning over 95% of spurious un-kitted branching combinations; Stage 2 executes local fine-grained sorting and swapping on Intensive Capacities exclusively within the narrowed kitted feasible window in log-linear time 𝒪(𝑁 log𝑁)-combined with a finite causal propagation depth 𝐾 bounded by the physical instability window, factorial 𝒪(𝑁!) explosion collapses into deterministic polynomial-time closed-loop computability 𝑇 step (𝑁) = 𝒪(𝐾 ⋅ 𝑁 log𝑁) ∈ 𝑷 (with physical wall-clock runtime 𝑇 wall (𝑁) = 𝑐 hw ⋅ 𝑇 step (𝑁) ≤ 𝜏 phy < +∞). Third, because the effective control dimension is bounded by the observable and writable feedback dimension (dim𝒞 ≤ dim𝒪), engineering construction must follow the Dual-Direction Construction Principle: strategic guardrails Top-Down, closed-loop capability foundation Bottom-Up. Implemented in the general-purpose Intelligent Planning & Control (IPC) Engine, this law solves 500,000 demand orders, a 20-level BOM, and 2,000,000 material items in 296 seconds on a single commodity PC.

detail.abstract: Option desks and practitioners read the price of the at-the-money straddle as the move the market expects by expiry. We test that reading on the Nasdaq-100. For every trading day from January 2019 to April 2026 and for five constant tenors between one day and three months, we compare the expected move implied by QQQ options (ATM straddle divided by the forward) with the absolute return the Nasdaq-100 then realizes over the same window, for a total of 7,893 implied/realized pairs. detail.abstract: Price limits protect orderly trading worldwide, yet they may change how news reaches prices, which matters for regulators. This study examines how regulator-imposed price floors on the Dhaka Stock Exchange change the way Bangla financial-news tone is reflected in returns and trading activity, and whether tone accumulated during a floor is released once the floor is lifted.
